question: On a low-voltage power breaker, ATS 7.6.1.2 lists long-time, short-time, ground-fault, and instantaneous pickup as primary-injection tests. Secondary injection is:
choices: Marked optional, and it is not the method named for those four pickup tests
The only acceptable method for electronic trip units
explanation: B.3 through B.6 say determine those functions by primary current injection. B.7, secondary injection, carries the optional asterisk. Secondary injection does not pass current through the sensors and the poles.

question: Which item is an electrical test in ATS 7.6.1.2, not a visual and mechanical inspection item?
choices: Compare the nameplate with the drawings
Confirm settings match the coordination study
explanation: Contact resistance is in the electrical-test list (B.2), with its limit in D.2. Nameplate comparison, torque, and the coordination-study settings check sit in the visual and mechanical section. NETA wording traps hang on that split.

question: No manufacturer curve is available. A molded-case breaker rated 100 A, 480 V, is tested at 300% of continuous rating. Table 100.7 maximum trip time is:
explanation: The 51–100 A row and the 251–600 V column is 160 seconds. The ≤250 V column on that row is 140 seconds. 50 seconds is the 0–30 A, ≤250 V cell. The table is specifically the 300% test.

question: Control-wiring insulation resistance on a low-voltage power breaker shall not be less than:
explanation: ATS 7.6.1.2.D.3 states 2 MΩ for control wiring. The 100 MΩ figure is the Table 100.1 floor for 600 V power insulation, not the control-wire floor.

question: Which auxiliary feature does ATS 7.6.1.2.B.8 tell you to verify on a low-voltage power breaker?
choices: Turns ratio of the power transformer
explanation: The list includes trip and pickup indicators, zone interlocking, electrical close and trip, trip-free, antipump, and the trip-unit battery. Oil tests, TTR, and soil boxes are other sections.

question: Trip-free operation means:
choices: The breaker cannot trip while a lockout relay is picked up
The breaker will trip even if the close command is held
The closing spring will recharge while the trip coil is energized
Antipump has been defeated on purpose
explanation: Trip-free is the ability to trip even if close is held, so a fault during a close still opens the breaker. Antipump is the separate function that prevents a second close until the close signal is removed and reasserted. ATS tells you to verify both; it does not define them in that sentence. The definitions are the mechanism behavior.

question: Adjustable instantaneous trip, field tolerance. ATS-2025 Table 100.8 versus MTS-2023 Table 100.8:
explanation: Electronic trip units are +30% / −30% in both tables. Adjustable units are ±40% in ATS-2025 and +40% / −30% in MTS-2023. The ±25% figures apply to nonadjustable breakers, measured outside the published band, not to the adjustable setting.
reference: ANSI/NETA ATS-2025 Table 100.8; ANSI/NETA MTS-2023 Table 100.8

question: An electronic trip unit's instantaneous setting is tested in the field with no manufacturer tolerance in hand. Which band applies in both ATS-2025 and MTS-2023 Table 100.8?
explanation: Electronic trip units are +30% and −30% of the setting in both tables. The adjustable +40% row is a different breaker type. Putting the adjustable band on an electronic unit is the table miss.
reference: ANSI/NETA ATS-2025 Table 100.8; ANSI/NETA MTS-2023 Table 100.8

question: Table 100.12.1, cadmium- or zinc-plated steel, 1/2 inch SAE grade 5. Torque is:
explanation: Grade 5, 1/2 inch, is 48 pound-feet. Grade 1 and 2 at that diameter are 30. Grade 8 is 74. The head mark has to match the column, and metric bolts are not this table.

question: Main-tie-main, both mains closed, tie open, loads split. An operator closes the tie and then opens main A. What did that sequence do to the bus that had been fed by main A?
choices: It kept that bus energized from main B through the tie, provided the tie closed first and stayed closed
It de-energized the main B bus
It automatically transfers the ground relay to the other main
explanation: Order matters. Closing the tie while both mains are still closed briefly parallels the two sources, which is a closed transition. Opening main A after that leaves the former A-bus loads fed from main B through the tie. Main B itself stays closed, so the sequence does not de-energize the main B bus. Many main-tie-main schemes block that parallel with a two-out-of-three interlock, or allow it only under sync-check. Open the tie first, or open main A while the tie is still open, and the A bus goes dark. Confirm the interlocks on the actual schematic before operating.
reference: Engineering fundamentals (main-tie-main operation); ANSI/NETA ATS-2025 Section 8

question: A key interlock between a grounding switch and the live switch keeps the two from being closed at the same time, so the grounding switch cannot close onto a live bus. Someone cuts a second key to the same code. The scheme:
choices: Still enforces the sequence, because the lock manufacturer registered the code
Is defeated; a spare identical key lets both locks be operated
Becomes stronger, because two keys provide redundancy
Only fails if the key is made of aluminum
explanation: The interlock works because there is one key, so the grounding switch and the live switch cannot both be closed. A duplicate lets an operator release both mechanisms. Key control is part of the procedure. The lock cannot police a second key by itself.

question: Zone-selective interlocking is listed in ATS 7.6.1.2.B.8 as something you verify. In the usual scheme, a restraint signal from the downstream breaker causes the upstream breaker to:
choices: Wait on its delayed setting while the downstream device is expected to clear; with no restraint it may trip on the faster unrestrained time
Raise its sensor rating to the frame size
explanation: The standard requires the function test. The logic — downstream restraint holds the upstream short-time or ground element on its longer delay, and loss of restraint releases the faster trip — is the scheme you are proving. Confirm the exact behavior in that trip unit's manual.
reference: ANSI/NETA ATS-2025 7.6.1.2.B.8; Eaton Digitrip 1150+ instruction leaflet IL70C1036H06, zone interlocking

question: A single-pole primary shot on a four-pole breaker with residual ground fault will often:
choices: Look like a ground fault and trip the ground element
Read as a healthy three-phase load
explanation: One pole in and nowhere out is residual current, which is what the ground function is built to see. Run the return through the neutral pole, or raise the ground function the way that manual allows, then put the settings back.
reference: Eaton Digitrip 1150+ instruction leaflet IL70C1036H06, Section 5; ANSI/NETA ATS-2025 7.6.1.2.B.5

question: The trip-unit manual publishes an instantaneous tolerance. ATS 7.6.1.2 says you:
choices: Ignore the manual and use Table 100.8 anyway
Use the published tolerance; Table 100.8 applies only in the absence of manufacturer data
explanation: Instantaneous pickup shall be as specified and within the manufacturer’s published tolerances. Table 100.8 is the fallback when that data does not exist. A manual that says ±10% is a tighter or different story than the adjustable molded-case band.

question: Short-time timing is short, about a few cycles, and zone-interlock restraint was never jumpered. The likely cause is:
choices: The element tripped unrestrained because no restraint signal was present
explanation: Without a restraint jumper, short-time and ground are allowed to trip on the fast unrestrained time. That is what the scheme does in service when the downstream breaker is not holding them off. Jumper only for the delayed-band shot, then remove it and restore settings.
reference: Eaton Digitrip 1150+ instruction leaflet IL70C1036H06, zone-interlocking restraint jumper; ANSI/NETA ATS-2025 7.6.1.2.B.8

question: On an Eaton PXR 20/25, the long-delay time dial is defined at:
explanation: The protection table in the PXR 20/25 user manual labels long delay time at 6 times Ir. A shot at some other multiple is not that dial unless you are on the published curve. Do not treat a hand-scaled time as the acceptance window.
reference: Eaton PXR 20/25 user manual, per manufacturer instructions

question: Long-time memory on a PXR trip unit matters during primary injection because:
choices: Repeated overload shots can stack and change the next trip
explanation: The PXR manual includes long-time memory so repeated overloads are not ignored. For a string of timing shots, turn that memory off if the manual tells you to, then turn it back on and restore the as-found settings.
reference: Eaton PXR 20/25 user manual, per manufacturer instructions

question: Instantaneous pickup on a PXR is a multiple of:
choices: In, the sensor or rating plug
explanation: The PXR protection table lists instantaneous as a multiple of In, while short-time pickup is a multiple of Ir. Mixing In and Ir moves the test current by a lot when the plug is not full frame.
reference: Eaton PXR 20/25 user manual, per manufacturer instructions

question: Short-time pickup on a PXR is a multiple of Ir, while instantaneous is a multiple of In. If the plug is 800 A in a 1600 A frame and Ir is 1.0, a 6× short-time pickup is:
explanation: Ir = 1.0 × 800 = 800 A. Short-time at 6 × Ir is 4800 A. Instantaneous multiples use In, which on this unit is the plug, 800 A, not the 1600 A frame. Read which symbol the dial says before you set the injection current.
reference: Eaton PXR 20/25 user manual, per manufacturer instructions

question: Ground-fault delay on a PXR that is labeled at 0.625 × In means the time dial is defined:
choices: At 0.625 times sensor rating, not at an arbitrary current you happened to inject
Only when zone interlock is on
explanation: The manual’s ground I²t times are at 0.625 × In. A shot at some other current is a different point on the curve. Confirm that point in the manufacturer’s curve before you fail the trip unit.
reference: Eaton PXR 20/25 user manual, per manufacturer instructions

question: Zone interlock is enabled and you are timing the delayed short-time band. The restraint input is open. You should expect:
choices: A fast, unrestrained trip, so the delayed window will not show until restraint is jumpered
explanation: No restraint means the downstream device is not holding this one back, which is exactly when the scheme is supposed to be fast. Jumper the restraint the way the manual shows, take the delayed shot, then remove the jumper and restore settings.
reference: Eaton PXR 20/25 user manual, per manufacturer instructions (zone interlock); ATS-2025 7.6.1.2.B.8

question: ATS switch inspection says fuse sizes must agree with:
choices: The largest fuse that fits the clips
The drawings and the coordination study
explanation: 7.5.1.1 checks fuse size and type against the drawings and the study, and it checks that each fuse is supported and has contact integrity. It does not publish a maximum insulation resistance between fuses. Higher insulation resistance is not a failure.

question: A 0.5 A fuse is going to be checked for continuity. The test current should be:
choices: 10 A, because that is a standard ductor range
Below the fuse rating so the test does not open it
The instantaneous pickup of the breaker ahead of it
explanation: ATS checks fuse support and contact. It does not tell you to push 10 A through a half-amp fuse. Stay under the fuse rating. The recalled meter-range choices are not in the specification.

question: Antipump, which ATS requires you to prove on a power breaker, means:
choices: The breaker will close and trip repeatedly while the close signal is held
One close attempt for a maintained close signal; it will not hammer
The charging motor is supposed to run continuously
explanation: Trip-free means it will trip even if close is held. Antipump means it will not reclose over and over while that close signal stays picked up. ATS 7.6.1.3 tests both, with the breaker in the test position, and the test values say those features shall function as designed. A charging motor that stays hot is a reason to prove this, not a reason to keep holding close.

question: Secondary control checks on a medium-voltage breaker, ATS 7.6.1.3, are made:
choices: With the breaker racked in and closed on the bus
In the test position: close and trip from the control switch, and trip from each protective relay
Only with the trip plugs pulled
explanation: The test position lets you operate the mechanism without putting the breaker on the bus. You also prove charge, trip-free, and antipump. Racking a closed breaker into the gear is what the interlock is there to stop.

question: A closed breaker that will not rack into the switchgear is showing:
choices: A failed trip unit that must be primary-injected on the bus
The racking interlock, which requires the breaker to be open
explanation: ATS has you prove interlocks by trying the blocked operation. A closed breaker is not supposed to rack in. Open it, then rack. Do not defeat the interlock to finish the job.

question: Bolt grade is identified in the field by:
choices: Head markings (see the grade row of ATS Table 100.12.1)
explanation: Bolt grade is read from the marks on the head. ATS-2025 Table 100.12.1 puts a head-marking row with the torque values, so the grade and the torque table sit together. Table 100.1, the glove class, and the polarization-index minimum do not identify bolt grade.

question: ATS 7.5 switch tests measure contact resistance:
choices: Only from the fuse to the station ground grid
As a maximum insulation resistance between fuses
With a 10 kV megohmmeter as the only instrument
explanation: The fuseholder and the blade are current-carrying joints. Compare them with similar joints. The section does not set a maximum insulation resistance between fuses. Fuse size still has to match the drawings and the study.

question: NFPA 70B-2026 Table 15.3.5 places the inverse-time trip test of a low-voltage breaker at:
choices: 150 percent of the frame size, regardless of the plug
explanation: The maintenance table calls for the inverse-time test at 300 percent of rated continuous current, and it also lists instantaneous. It does not print a trip-time band. That time still comes from the manufacturer or from the NETA table that applies to the test you are actually running.

question: NFPA 70B-2026 Table 15.3.4 says low-voltage breakers are operated:
choices: Once, then left alone for the rest of the cycle
Only if the instantaneous test fails
explanation: The servicing table includes operating the breaker at least three times, along with torque and interlock checks. Three operations are not a substitute for the electrical tests in the next table, and they are not a numeric contact-resistance limit.

question: NFPA 70B-2026 Table 15.4.5 says not to run an overpotential test on:
choices: The power poles of a medium-voltage breaker, ever
Control wiring that is connected to solid-state components
explanation: Medium-voltage breaker maintenance can include an enhanced overpotential test of the power circuit. Control wiring tied to solid-state parts is excluded from that overpotential test. Follow the manufacturer for those circuits instead of forcing a high-voltage test through the electronics.

question: Chapter 15 of NFPA 70B-2026 splits breaker scope at about:
choices: Low-voltage breakers through 1000 V, and medium-voltage power breakers above 1000 V through 69 kV
All breakers as one table with one test list
explanation: Molded-case, insulated-case, and low-voltage power breakers are the 1000 V and below group. Medium-voltage power breakers are the group above 1000 V through 69 kV. The two groups do not share one test list. Vacuum wear, oil, and gas condition show up on the medium-voltage inspection, not on a 480 V molded-case breaker.

question: Which test is on the low-voltage breaker list in NFPA 70B-2026 Table 15.3.5 and is not the headline of the medium-voltage list?
choices: Inverse-time trip at 300 percent of rated continuous current
Contact timing of a medium-voltage mechanism
Enhanced overpotential of the power circuit
explanation: The low-voltage electrical table includes thermography, contact resistance, insulation resistance, controls, electronic-trip calibration, the 300 percent inverse-time test, and instantaneous. The medium-voltage table instead stresses trip and close, mechanism, vacuum integrity, contact timing, and an enhanced overpotential test. Do not run a molded-case 300 percent shot and call it a vacuum-bottle test.

question: NFPA 70B-2026 Table 15.3.5 splits molded-case breaker columns at:
choices: Frames of 225 A and below versus larger frames, without printing trip-time seconds
A 1000 V versus 69 kV insulation test
explanation: The low-voltage electrical table separates molded-case frames of 225 A and below from larger frames. Both still see the inverse-time test at 300 percent of rated continuous current. The table does not give the seconds. That time is the manufacturer’s, or the NETA table if you are running an acceptance or maintenance test that actually publishes one.
